title: What a Reverse Proxy Does for a Website
content:
When a browser opens a website, the request may reach a gateway before it reaches the application. That gateway is a reverse proxy: it accepts a client request and forwards it to an upstream server, then returns the response. The proxy can choose an upstream, handle TLS, serve static assets, or apply routing rules. Each capability depends on configuration; the word “proxy” alone does not mean the site has all of them.

Trace one request through the gateway

Suppose a visitor requests /articles/42 over HTTPS. DNS points the browser toward the public endpoint. A reverse proxy accepts the connection, matches the host and path, forwards the request to the application server, receives the result, and sends it back. NGINX's reverse-proxy guide documents passing requests to an upstream and controlling forwarded headers. The application may run on a private port that browsers never contact directly.

The proxy sits on the server side of this conversation. A forward proxy, by comparison, is chosen to represent clients reaching external sites. A content delivery network may also proxy requests at an edge, but it has different placement and operating concerns. Use a network diagram with actual hostnames and ports to avoid arguing from labels. In one deployment, a cloud load balancer, edge service, and local NGINX instance may all sit in the request path.

Check how the original host, scheme, and client address reach the application. The NGINX proxy module documents proxy_pass and proxy_set_header directives. If forwarded headers are wrong or untrusted, an app may generate HTTP links behind an HTTPS proxy, misidentify the client, or accept spoofed address information. Configure a clear trust boundary: only the known proxy should supply authoritative forwarding metadata, and the app should trust only that hop.

Understand routing and TLS

A reverse proxy can route /api to an API server and /assets to static files or another service. It can also choose among multiple upstream instances. That flexibility is useful for gradual migration and scaling, but each route needs a documented owner and failure behavior. A request matching the wrong location rule may return a 404 or reach an unexpected service. Verify routing with representative paths, including trailing slashes and query strings.

TLS can terminate at the proxy, which means the browser's encrypted connection ends there. The hop from proxy to upstream may be local HTTP or another encrypted connection. State the actual network boundary and threat model. “The site uses HTTPS” describes the browser-facing segment; it does not prove that every internal hop is encrypted. Certificates, renewal, redirects, and secure cookie behavior should be checked at the public endpoint as well as in application settings.

A proxy can cache selected responses, compress content, or impose size and timeout limits. These features can improve delivery or break an application if configured without regard to dynamic behavior. Caching a private account page is a serious mistake. A low request-body limit may reject uploads while small forms succeed. A short upstream timeout may produce a gateway error even when the app eventually finishes. Treat each setting as a decision with a test case.

Read errors at the right layer

A 502 often means the proxy could not get a valid response from the upstream. A 504 commonly indicates an upstream timeout. These status codes narrow the boundary, but the cause can be a stopped process, wrong port, DNS failure, firewall rule, protocol mismatch, or slow dependency. Compare proxy access and error logs with application logs for the same request time. A healthy local app endpoint does not prove the public route is configured correctly.

Verify the active listener and upstream rather than editing the first configuration file you find. Multiple site files, containers, and load balancers can coexist. Check which process owns the public port, which configuration it loaded, and where the upstream actually runs. In a production change, test configuration syntax before reload and preserve a rollback path. A safe reload still needs a public-path check after it completes.

Log enough to trace a request across layers: timestamp, host, path, status, upstream address, upstream status, and a safe request identifier where supported. Avoid logging tokens or sensitive query strings. If the application sees an incorrect client IP, investigate the forwarding chain before changing rate limits or audit logic. A proxy is part of security and observability, not merely a traffic switch.

Hypothetical example: the homepage works, API fails

Imagine a hypothetical site whose homepage loads but every /api request returns 502. The proxy serves static files for /, while /api forwards to localhost:4000. The application container moved to a new internal port during deployment, and the proxy still points to the old one. A local request to the new app port works, confirming the app can respond, but the public path remains broken until the proxy upstream is corrected.

The operator checks the active config, tests the corrected route in a staging or controlled environment, reloads the proxy, and verifies both the homepage and an authenticated API path from outside. This is a hypothetical diagnostic path, not evidence about a real site. It shows why a working frontend and a working app process can coexist with a broken link between them.

Checklist for understanding a deployment

  • Identify the public hostname, listener, and active proxy process.
  • Map each relevant path to its upstream service and port.
  • Check TLS termination and encryption on later hops.
  • Verify forwarded headers and the app's trusted-proxy settings.
  • Review cache, body-size, timeout, and error behavior for dynamic routes.
  • Correlate proxy and upstream logs using time or request ID.
  • Test representative public paths after any routing change.

A reverse proxy makes a website's public address independent of its internal services. Its value lies in explicit routing and a well-understood boundary. Draw the actual path, verify each hop, and a gateway error becomes a tractable question instead of a mystery attributed to “the server.”
excerpt: Understand a website reverse proxy by tracing the public request through routing, TLS, forwarded headers, upstreams, and response handling.
